item.title: The Dance Class
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: Degas is filed under Impressionism, but he stood apart from the plein-air painters — a draftsman obsessed with line, artificial light, and the working body. He haunted the Paris Opéra not for performances but for rehearsals, and here the great ballet master Jules Perrot leans on his staff mid-correction while a dancer prepares her position and the rest of the class does what people actually do: stretches, fidgets, scratches, adjusts an earring, ignores everything. A little dog stands on the floorboards. This is ballet as labor — young working-class girls, many supporting families, under an old master's eye — not as spectacle. The composition is pure Degas: the floor rushing away in a steep diagonal, figures sliced by the frame like a candid photograph, empty space given the best seat. He claimed, 'no art was ever less spontaneous than mine'; every offhand-looking pose here was calculated from dozens of drawings.
item.lookFor: Find the dancer seated on the piano at left, scratching her back — the least classical pose in art's most famous ballet picture, and the detail that tells you Degas cared more about truth than grace.
